Title: Beyond the Dashboard: Rethinking Observability for Event-Driven Systems

More organizations are adopting event-driven architectures, and traditional monitoring approaches are struggling to keep pace with the complexity of asynchronous workflows.

This talk shares what we learned migrating Corvid Pay's payment pipeline from a request-response model to an event-driven one built on Kafka. Over 18 months, our team reduced mean time to detection from 27 minutes to under 4 and cut alerting noise by roughly 60%. The tools were only part of it. We also had to rethink how we understand system behavior.

Attendees will learn:

- How to trace a single payment across 14 services using OpenTelemetry context propagation
- Why we abandoned per-service dashboards in favor of event-flow views
- Practical strategies for sampling high-volume topics without losing rare failures

Whether you're just starting with event-driven systems or looking to improve an existing observability practice, you'll leave with techniques you can apply right away.

Speaker: Leah Okonkwo-Brandt, Staff Engineer, Corvid Pay
Session length: 40 minutes

Harbor at Dusk, 1958
Oil on canvas
Agnes Thorvaldsen (American, born Norway, 1911–1987)
Gift of the Wendell Family, 1994

Agnes Thorvaldsen painted *Harbor at Dusk* during her final summer in Gloucester, Massachusetts. It catches the moment when daylight gives way to evening and the working harbor turns violet and amber.

Thorvaldsen emigrated from Bergen at the age of nine and often spoke of the harbors of her childhood. Here, those memories seem to merge with the New England present. The loose, gestural brushwork reflects her growing interest in Abstract Expressionism, while the recognizable masts and pier keep the composition anchored in observed reality.

She applied the paint for the water with a palette knife, building up ridges that catch the gallery light and appear to move as viewers walk past. The painting was first exhibited at the Rockport Art Association in 1959, where it received the association's Gold Medal.

Place and identity run together in this picture: home is not merely a location, but a feeling we carry with us.

# Three Perfect Days in Ljubljana

Ljubljana sits between the Alps and the Adriatic, with old-world charm and a young, lively feel. Its center is car-free, dragons guard its bridges, and cafés line the river. Slovenia's capital works for history buffs, foodies, and outdoor types alike.

## Day 1: Old Town and the Castle

Start your morning at Prešeren Square, then cross the Triple Bridge into the Old Town. Ride the funicular up to Ljubljana Castle (€16 for the funicular and castle entry) and take in sweeping views of the red rooftops. In the evening, have dinner along the Ljubljanica River.

## Day 2: Lake Bled Day Trip

Catch the 8:00 a.m. bus from the main station; the ride takes about 1 hour 20 minutes. Walk the 6-kilometer loop around the lake, row a pletna boat to the island church, and don't leave without trying the famous cream cake.

## Day 3: Markets and Metelkova

Browse the Central Market (closed Sundays) for local cheeses and honey, then spend the afternoon exploring Metelkova, the city's colorful alternative arts district.

Ljubljana is small, but it leaves a big impression.

The *Halcyon* drifted in the silence of the outer belt, its hull ticking as it cooled. Commander Rhee floated before the viewport, watching the derelict probe tumble slowly against the stars.

"It's been out here for two hundred years," said Ito-Marsh, the ship's engineer, her voice barely above a whisper. "Two hundred years, and it's still transmitting."

Rhee's fingers went cold on the edge of the viewport frame. The signal was faint but unmistakable: the same three tones, repeating every eleven seconds.

"We have to bring it aboard," Ito-Marsh said. "Think about what we could learn."

"Or we leave it," Rhee replied. "Some things aren't meant to be found. Curiosity isn't just a gift — it's a responsibility."

The engineer was silent for a long moment. Then she nodded slowly. "You're right. It's not our story to finish."

Rhee turned back to the viewport. The probe's antenna caught the light of the distant sun, a single silver thread against the dark. Eleven seconds passed, and the three tones came again.

She marked the coordinates in the log and set a course for home.

- **Facts and voice.** The two hundred years, the three tones every eleven seconds, the argument, the coordinates and the course home are all unchanged. The dialogue is untouched. The one addition is a brief beat where the tones repeat, which fits the eleven-second interval already established.

Bought this kettle in March after our old one started leaking from the base. It's been six months, so here's where I've landed.

The good: it boils a full liter in a little under four minutes, the temperature presets actually match what my thermometer says (I checked 80, 90 and 100), and the keep-warm setting holds for 30 minutes before shutting off, which is longer than I expected. The handle stays cool. The lid opens with one thumb, which matters more than you'd think at 6 a.m.

The less good: the water window is on the back, facing the wall, so I have to turn the whole thing around to see how much is in it. And the base beeps three times every time you lift it off. You can turn the beep off, but it took me a week to find the setting (hold the minus button for five seconds, if anyone else is wondering).

Would I buy it again? Yes. It's not the prettiest kettle on the counter, but it does the one job I need it to do, and it does it every morning without fuss.

My father taught me to drive in the parking lot of a church that had closed the year before. He said it was the only flat, empty place in town where nobody would mind if I hit the curb, and I hit it more than once.

He was not a patient man in most things, but he was patient that summer. He never grabbed the wheel. When I stalled, which was often, he would wait for the engine to go quiet and then say, "Again," as if we had all the time in the world. Maybe we did, then.

The last lesson was in August. I drove the two miles home on real streets while he sat with his hands folded in his lap, looking out the window and pretending not to watch the speedometer. I parked in front of the house, badly, and he got out without a word and went inside.

I've been driving for thirty years now. I still check the mirrors the way he showed me, left, rearview, right, before I pull away from a curb. Some lessons don't need to be repeated to stay with you.

- **The closing line:** "Some lessons don't need to be repeated to stay with you" states the theme outright. It also quietly answers the father's "Again," and it rests on the mirror habit the paragraph just showed, so I left it.
- **"Humanize" as a goal:** I don't edit toward a "sounds human" target. Changing good sentences to make them seem less polished would make the piece worse. If you have a specific concern, such as the ending feeling too tidy, tell me and I'll look at that.

final: Then to my morning work. First I take an axe and pail and go in search of water, if that be not a dream. After a cold and snowy night it needed a divining rod to find it. Every winter the liquid and trembling surface of the pond, which was so sensitive to every breath, and reflected every light and shadow, becomes solid to the depth of a foot or a foot and a half, so that it will support the heaviest teams, and perchance the snow covers it to an equal depth, and it is not to be distinguished from any level field. Like the marmots in the surrounding hills, it closes its eye-lids and becomes dormant for three months or more. Standing on the snow-covered plain, as if in a pasture amid the hills, I cut my way first through a foot of snow, and then a foot of ice, and open a window under my feet, where, kneeling to drink, I look down into the quiet parlor of the fishes, pervaded by a softened light as through a window of ground glass, with its bright sanded floor the same as in summer; there a perennial waveless serenity reigns as in the amber twilight sky, corresponding to the cool and even temperament of the inhabitants. Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.

I found no concrete problem for a reader, and editing it would only flatten that voice, so I'm returning it unchanged.

If you meant a different text, or you want a modernized version for a particular audience (say, simpler syntax for students), tell me and I'll do that as an explicit transformation.

For instance, there is a current impression that it is unpleasant to have to run after one’s hat. Why should it be unpleasant to the well-ordered and pious mind? Not merely because it is running, and running exhausts one. The same people run much faster in games and sports. The same people run much more eagerly after an uninteresting little leather ball than they will after a nice silk hat. There is an idea that it is humiliating to run after one’s hat; and when people say it is humiliating they mean that it is comic. It certainly is comic; but man is a very comic creature, and most of the things he does are comic—eating, for instance. And the most comic things of all are exactly the things that are most worth doing—such as making love. A man running after a hat is not half so ridiculous as a man running after a wife.

Now a man could, if he felt rightly in the matter, run after his hat with the manliest ardour and the most sacred joy. He might regard himself as a jolly huntsman pursuing a wild animal, for certainly no animal could be wilder. In fact, I am inclined to believe that hat-hunting on windy days will be the sport of the upper classes in the future. There will be a meet of ladies and gentlemen on some high ground on a gusty morning. They will be told that the professional attendants have started a hat in such-and-such a thicket, or whatever be the technical term. Notice that this employment will in the fullest degree combine sport with humanitarianism. The hunters would feel that they were not inflicting pain. Nay, they would feel that they were inflicting pleasure, rich, almost riotous pleasure, upon the people who were looking on. When last I saw an old gentleman running after his hat in Hyde Park, I told him that a heart so benevolent as his ought to be filled with peace and thanks at the thought of how much unaffected pleasure his every gesture and bodily attitude were at that moment giving to the crowd.
reply:
I'd leave this one alone. It reads as a person's writing because it is one: it's the opening of G. K. Chesterton's "On Running After One's Hat" (1908). The voice is distinctive, the paradox builds on purpose ("man is a very comic creature… eating, for instance"), and the "Nay," and "or whatever be the technical term" asides are deliberate stance. I found no concrete problem for the reader, and rewriting it to seem more human would flatten what already works. I'm returning it unchanged, and I didn't run any scripts or checks.

<<<FINAL>>>

Not merely because it is running, and running exhausts one. The same people run much faster in games and sports. The same people run much more eagerly after an uninteresting little leather ball than they will after a nice silk hat. There is an idea that it is humiliating to run after one’s hat; and when people say it is humiliating they mean that it is comic. It certainly is comic; but man is a very comic creature, and most of the things he does are comic—eating, for instance. And the most comic things of all are exactly the things that are most worth doing—such as making love. A man running after a hat is not half so ridiculous as a man running after a wife.

Now a man could, if he felt rightly in the matter, run after his hat with the manliest ardour and the most sacred joy. He might regard himself as a jolly huntsman pursuing a wild animal, for certainly no animal could be wilder. In fact, I am inclined to believe that hat-hunting on windy days will be the sport of the upper classes in the future. There will be a meet of ladies and gentlemen on some high ground on a gusty morning. They will be told that the professional attendants have started a hat in such-and-such a thicket, or whatever be the technical term. Notice that this employment will in the fullest degree combine sport with humanitarianism. The hunters would feel that they were not inflicting pain. Nay, they would feel that they were inflicting pleasure, rich, almost riotous pleasure, upon the people who were looking on. When last I saw an old gentleman running after his hat in Hyde Park, I told him that a heart so benevolent as his ought to be filled with peace and thanks at the thought of how much unaffected pleasure his every gesture and bodily attitude were at that moment giving to the crowd.
<<<END>>>

Until the latest of our world conflicts, the United States had no armaments industry. American makers of plowshares could, with time and as required, make swords as well. But now we can no longer risk emergency improvisation of national defense; we have been compelled to create a permanent armaments industry of vast proportions. Added to this, three and a half million men and women are directly engaged in the defense establishment. We annually spend on military security more than the net income of all United States corporations.

This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience. The total influence—economic, political, even spiritual—is felt in every city, every state house, every office of the Federal government. We recognize the imperative need for this development. Yet we must not fail to comprehend its grave implications. Our toil, resources and livelihood are all involved; so is the very structure of our society.

In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.

We must never let the weight of this combination endanger our liberties or democratic processes. We should take nothing for granted. Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial and military machinery of defense with our peaceful methods and goals, so that security and liberty may prosper together.

Containers are a good way to bundle and run your applications. In a production environment, you need to manage the containers that run the applications and ensure that there is no downtime. For example, if a container goes down, another container needs to start. Wouldn't it be easier if a system handled this for you?

That's where Kubernetes comes in. It gives you a framework for running distributed systems resiliently. It takes care of scaling and failover for your application, provides deployment patterns, and more. For example, Kubernetes can easily manage a canary deployment for your system.

Kubernetes provides you with:

* **Service discovery and load balancing**
  Kubernetes can expose a container using a DNS name or its own IP address. If traffic to a container is high, Kubernetes can load balance and distribute the network traffic so that the deployment stays stable.
* **Storage orchestration**
  Kubernetes lets you automatically mount a storage system of your choice, such as local storage, public cloud providers, and more.
* **Automated rollouts and rollbacks**
  You can describe the desired state for your deployed containers using Kubernetes, and it can change the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate. For example, you can automate Kubernetes to create new containers for your deployment, remove existing containers and adopt all their resources into the new container.
* **Automatic bin packing**
  You give Kubernetes a cluster of nodes that it can use to run containerized tasks, and tell it how much CPU and memory (RAM) each container needs. Kubernetes can fit containers onto your nodes to make the best use of your resources.

Go’s treatment of errors as values has served us well over the last decade. Although the standard library’s support for errors has been minimal—just the `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf` functions, which produce errors that contain only a message—the built-in `error` interface allows Go programmers to add whatever information they desire. All it requires is a type that implements an `Error` method:

```go
type QueryError struct {
    Query string
    Err   error
}

func (e *QueryError) Error() string { return e.Query + ": " + e.Err.Error() }
```

Error types like this one are ubiquitous, and the information they store varies widely, from timestamps to filenames to server addresses. Often, that information includes another, lower-level error to provide additional context.

The pattern of one error containing another is so pervasive in Go code that, after extensive discussion, Go 1.13 added explicit support for it. This post describes the additions to the standard library that provide that support: three new functions in the `errors` package, and a new formatting verb for `fmt.Errorf`.

Before describing the changes in detail, let’s review how errors are examined and constructed in previous versions of the language.

Title: Beyond the Dashboard: Rethinking Observability for Event-Driven Systems

More teams are adopting event-driven architectures, and traditional monitoring is struggling to keep up with asynchronous workflows.

In this talk, I'll share what we learned migrating Corvid Pay's payment pipeline from a request-response model to an event-driven one built on Kafka. Over 18 months, our team cut mean time to detection from 27 minutes to under 4 and reduced alerting noise by roughly 60%. But the tools were only part of it. The bigger change was rethinking how we understand system behavior.

Attendees will learn:

- How to trace a single payment across 14 services using OpenTelemetry context propagation
- Why we abandoned per-service dashboards in favor of event-flow views
- Practical strategies for sampling high-volume topics without losing rare failures

Whether you're just starting with event-driven systems or want to improve the observability practice you already have, you'll leave with ideas you can use right away.

Speaker: Leah Okonkwo-Brandt, Staff Engineer, Corvid Pay
Session length: 40 minutes

Harbor at Dusk, 1958
Oil on canvas
Agnes Thorvaldsen (American, born Norway, 1911–1987)
Gift of the Wendell Family, 1994

Agnes Thorvaldsen painted *Harbor at Dusk* during her final summer in Gloucester, Massachusetts. It shows the moment when daylight gives way to evening and the working harbor turns violet and amber. Light, water, and memory were subjects she returned to throughout her career.

Thorvaldsen emigrated from Bergen at the age of nine and often spoke of the harbors of her childhood. In this painting, those memories seem to blend with the New England harbor in front of her. The loose, gestural brushwork reflects her growing interest in Abstract Expressionism, while the recognizable masts and pier keep the scene tied to what she saw.

She applied the paint for the water with a palette knife, building up ridges that catch the gallery light and seem to shift as viewers walk past. The painting was first exhibited at the Rockport Art Association in 1959, where it won the association's Gold Medal.

*Harbor at Dusk* is about place and identity. Home, it suggests, is more than a location. It is a feeling we carry with us.

# Three Perfect Days in Ljubljana

Ljubljana sits between the Alps and the Adriatic, and it manages to feel both old and young at once. The center is car-free, dragons guard the bridges, and the river is lined with cafés. Slovenia's capital suits history buffs, food lovers and anyone who likes being outdoors.

## Day 1: Old Town and the Castle

Start your morning at Prešeren Square, then cross the Triple Bridge into the Old Town. Ride the funicular up to Ljubljana Castle (€16 for the funicular and castle entry) and look out over the red rooftops. In the evening, have dinner along the Ljubljanica River.

## Day 2: Lake Bled Day Trip

Catch the 8:00 a.m. bus from the main station; the ride takes about 1 hour 20 minutes. Walk the 6-kilometer loop around the lake, row a pletna boat to the island church, and don't leave without trying the famous cream cake.

## Day 3: Markets and Metelkova

Browse the Central Market (closed Sundays) for local cheeses and honey, then spend the afternoon exploring Metelkova, the city's colorful alternative arts district.

Ljubljana is small, but it leaves a big impression.

The *Halcyon* drifted in the silence of the outer belt, its hull ticking as it cooled. Commander Rhee floated before the viewport, watching the derelict probe tumble slowly against the stars.

"It's been out here two hundred years," said Ito-Marsh, the ship's engineer, her voice barely above a whisper. "Two hundred years, and it's still transmitting."

Rhee's stomach tightened. The signal was faint but unmistakable: the same three tones, repeating every eleven seconds.

"We have to bring it aboard," Ito-Marsh said. "Think about what we could learn."

"Or we leave it," Rhee said. "Some things aren't meant to be found. Curiosity is a gift, but it's a responsibility too."

The engineer was quiet for a long moment. Then she nodded. "You're right. It's not our story to finish."

Rhee turned back to the viewport. The probe's antenna caught the light of the distant sun, a single silver thread against the dark. She understood then that the universe was something to witness, not to conquer.

She marked the coordinates in the log and set a course for home.

Bought this kettle in March after our old one started leaking from the base. It's been six months, so here's where I've landed.

The good: it boils a full liter in a little under four minutes, the temperature presets actually match what my thermometer says (I checked 80, 90 and 100), and the keep-warm setting holds for 30 minutes before shutting off, which is longer than I expected. The handle stays cool. The lid opens with one thumb, which matters more than you'd think at 6 a.m.

The less good: the water window is on the back, facing the wall, so I have to turn the whole thing around to see how much is in it. And the base beeps three times every time you lift it off. You can turn the beep off, but it took me a week to find the setting (hold the minus button for five seconds, if anyone else is wondering).

Would I buy it again? Yes. It's not the prettiest kettle on the counter, but it does the one job I need it to do, and it does it every morning without fuss.

My father taught me to drive in the parking lot of a church that had closed the year before. He said it was the only flat, empty place in town where nobody would mind if I hit the curb, and I hit it more than once.

He was not a patient man in most things, but he was patient that summer. He never grabbed the wheel. When I stalled, which was often, he would wait for the engine to go quiet and then say, "Again," as if we had all the time in the world. Maybe we did, then.

The last lesson was in August. I drove the two miles home on real streets while he sat with his hands folded in his lap, looking out the window and pretending not to watch the speedometer. I parked in front of the house, badly, and he got out without a word and went inside.

I've been driving for thirty years now. I still check the mirrors the way he showed me, left, rearview, right, before I pull away from a curb. Some lessons don't need to be repeated to stay with you.

For instance, there is a current impression that it is unpleasant to have to run after one's hat. Why should it be unpleasant to the well-ordered and pious mind? Not merely because it is running, and running exhausts one. The same people run much faster in games and sports. The same people run much more eagerly after an uninteresting little leather ball than they will after a nice silk hat. There is an idea that it is humiliating to run after one's hat; and when people say it is humiliating they mean that it is comic. It certainly is comic; but man is a very comic creature, and most of the things he does are comic—eating, for instance. And the most comic things of all are exactly the things that are most worth doing—such as making love. A man running after a hat is not half so ridiculous as a man running after a wife.

Now a man could, if he felt rightly in the matter, run after his hat with the manliest ardour and the most sacred joy. He might regard himself as a jolly huntsman pursuing a wild animal, for certainly no animal could be wilder. In fact, I am inclined to believe that hat-hunting on windy days will be the sport of the upper classes in the future. There will be a meet of ladies and gentlemen on some high ground on a gusty morning. They will be told that the professional attendants have started a hat in such-and-such a thicket, or whatever be the technical term. Notice that this employment will in the fullest degree combine sport with humanitarianism. The hunters would feel that they were not inflicting pain. Nay, they would feel that they were inflicting pleasure, rich, almost riotous pleasure, upon the people who were looking on. When last I saw an old gentleman running after his hat in Hyde Park, I told him that a heart so benevolent as his ought to be filled with peace and thanks at the thought of how much unaffected pleasure his every gesture and bodily attitude were at that moment giving to the crowd.

I have just read yours of the 19th instant, addressed to myself through the "New York Tribune."

If there be in it any statements or assumptions of fact which I may know to be erroneous, I do not now and here controvert them.

If there be in it any inferences which I may believe to be falsely drawn, I do not now and here argue against them.

If there be perceptible in it an impatient and dictatorial tone, I waive it, in deference to an old friend whose heart I have always supposed to be right.

As to the policy I "seem to be pursuing," as you say, I have not meant to leave any one in doubt. I would save the Union. I would save it in the shortest way under the Constitution.

The sooner the national authority can be restored, the nearer the Union will be,—the Union as it was.

If there be those who would not save the Union unless they could at the same time save slavery, I do not agree with them.

If there be those who would not save the Union unless they could at the same time destroy slavery, I do not agree with them.

*My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and not either to save or to destroy slavery.*

If I could save the Union without freeing any slave, I would do it; if I could save it by freeing all the slaves, I would do it; and if I could save it by freeing some and leaving others alone, I would also do that.

What I do about slavery and the coloured race, I do because I believe it helps to save the Union; and what I forbear, I forbear because I do not believe it would help to save the Union.

I shall do less whenever I shall believe that what I am doing hurts the cause; and I shall do more whenever I shall believe doing more will help the cause.

I shall try to correct errors where shown to be errors, and I shall adopt new views as fast as they shall appear to be true views.

I have here stated my purpose according to my views of official duty, and I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.

Until the latest of our world conflicts, the United States had no armaments industry. American makers of plowshares could, with time and as required, make swords as well. But now we can no longer risk emergency improvisation of national defense; we have been compelled to create a permanent armaments industry of vast proportions. Added to this, three and a half million men and women are directly engaged in the defense establishment. We annually spend on military security more than the net income of all United States corporations.

This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience. The total influence—economic, political, even spiritual—is felt in every city, every state house, every office of the Federal government. We recognize the imperative need for this development. Yet we must not fail to comprehend its grave implications. Our toil, resources and livelihood are all involved; so is the very structure of our society.

In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.

We must never let the weight of this combination endanger our liberties or democratic processes. We should take nothing for granted. Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial and military machinery of defense with our peaceful methods and goals, so that security and liberty may prosper together.

Containers are a great way to bundle and run your applications. In production, you have to manage the containers that run those applications and make sure there's no downtime. If a container goes down, for example, another one needs to start. Wouldn't it be easier if a system handled this for you?

That's where Kubernetes comes in. It gives you a framework for running distributed systems resiliently. It takes care of scaling and failover for your application, provides deployment patterns, and more. It can, for instance, easily manage a canary deployment for your system.

Kubernetes gives you:

* **Service discovery and load balancing**
  Kubernetes can expose a container using a DNS name or its own IP address. If traffic to a container is high, Kubernetes can load balance and distribute the network traffic so the deployment stays stable.
* **Storage orchestration**
  Kubernetes lets you automatically mount the storage system of your choice, such as local storage, a public cloud provider, and more.
* **Automated rollouts and rollbacks**
  You describe the desired state for your deployed containers, and Kubernetes changes the actual state to match it at a controlled rate. For example, you can automate Kubernetes to create new containers for your deployment, remove existing containers, and move all their resources over to the new ones.
* **Automatic bin packing**
  You give Kubernetes a cluster of nodes to run containerized tasks on, and tell it how much CPU and memory (RAM) each container needs. Kubernetes then fits containers onto your nodes to make the best use of your resources.

Go’s treatment of errors as values has served us well over the last decade. Although the standard library’s support for errors has been minimal—just the `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf` functions, which produce errors that contain only a message—the built-in `error` interface allows Go programmers to add whatever information they desire. All it requires is a type that implements an `Error` method:

```go
type QueryError struct {
    Query string
    Err   error
}

func (e *QueryError) Error() string { return e.Query + ": " + e.Err.Error() }
```

Error types like this one are ubiquitous, and the information they store varies widely, from timestamps to filenames to server addresses. Often, that information includes another, lower-level error to provide additional context.

The pattern of one error containing another is so pervasive in Go code that, after extensive discussion, Go 1.13 added explicit support for it. This post describes the additions to the standard library that provide that support: three new functions in the `errors` package, and a new formatting verb for `fmt.Errorf`.

Before describing the changes in detail, let’s review how errors are examined and constructed in previous versions of the language.

## Getting Started

**lintwise** is a configurable linter for YAML files. Whether you're managing Kubernetes manifests or CI pipelines, it helps you catch errors before they reach production.

### Installation

lintwise requires Python 3.10 or later. Install it with pip:

```bash
pip install lintwise
```

### Usage

Point lintwise at a file or directory:

```bash
lintwise check ./config
```

By default, lintwise checks indentation, duplicate keys, and trailing whitespace. You can customize the rules by creating a `.lintwise.toml` file in your project root. lintwise exits with code 1 if it finds any errors, so you can use it in your CI workflow.

Last spring, at thirty-four, I finally decided to learn how to swim. For years I had avoided pools, lakes, and beaches, quietly ashamed of a skill everyone else seemed to have picked up as children. Signing up for adult lessons at the YMCA felt like a small act of courage.

The first class was humbling. I clung to the wall while an eight-year-old swam laps in the next lane. My instructor, Gloria, a patient retired teacher, told me to put my face in the water and blow bubbles. My heart pounded. It felt impossible.

But week by week, things changed. By June I could swim one slow length of freestyle without stopping. It wasn't pretty, but it was mine.

Learning to swim taught me something more important than a physical skill: it's never too late to face your fears, and growth begins at the edge of your comfort zone.

Daniel didn't turn around. "The bank isn't giving us a choice. Dad left us more debt than trees."

Marcus had to swallow before he answered. "This orchard was his whole life. It's where we grew up. It's not just land, Danny. It's who we are."

"Okay," Marcus finally said. "But I'm keeping his pruning shears."

Daniel laughed, a small, broken sound, and Marcus knew they would be all right.

Welcome to _The Rust Programming Language_, an introductory book about Rust. The Rust programming language helps you write faster, more reliable software. High-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds in programming language design; Rust challenges that conflict. By balancing powerful technical capacity and a great developer experience, Rust gives you the option to control low-level details (such as memory usage) without all the hassle traditionally associated with such control.

## Who Rust Is For

Rust is ideal for many people for a variety of reasons. Let’s look at a few of the most important groups.

### Teams of Developers

Rust is proving to be a productive tool for collaboration among large teams of developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge. Low-level code is prone to various subtle bugs, which in most other languages can only be caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced developers. In Rust, the compiler plays a gatekeeper role by refusing to compile code with these elusive bugs, including concurrency bugs. By working alongside the compiler, the team can spend its time focusing on the program’s logic rather than chasing down bugs.

Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:

- Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding, compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust ecosystem.
- The `rustfmt` formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across developers.
- The Rust Language Server powers integrated development environment (IDE) integration for code completion and inline error messages.

By using these and other tools in the Rust ecosystem, developers can be productive while writing systems-level code.

The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is *always* hungry.

He is always poor, out of luck and friendless. The meanest creatures despise him, and even the fleas would desert him for a velocipede. He is so spiritless and cowardly that even while his exposed teeth are pretending a threat, the rest of his face is apologizing for it. And he is so *homely*!—so scrawny, and ribby, and coarse-haired, and pitiful. When he sees you he lifts his lip and lets a flash of his teeth out, and then turns a little out of the course he was pursuing, depresses his head a bit, and strikes a long, soft-footed trot through the sage-brush, glancing over his shoulder at you, from time to time, till he is about out of easy pistol range, and then he stops and takes a deliberate survey of you; he will trot fifty yards and stop again—another fifty and stop again; and finally the gray of his gliding body blends with the gray of the sage-brush, and he disappears. All this is when you make no demonstration against him; but if you do, he develops a livelier interest in his journey, and instantly electrifies his heels and puts such a deal of real estate between himself and your weapon, that by the time you have raised the hammer you see that you need a minie rifle, and by the time you have got him in line you need a rifled cannon, and by the time you have “drawn a bead” on him you see well enough that nothing but an unusually long-winded streak of lightning could reach him where he is now. But if you start a swift-footed dog after him, you will enjoy it ever so much—especially if it is a dog that has a good opinion of himself, and has been brought up to think he knows something about speed.

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Finding time to cook a nourishing meal on a weeknight is hard. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta is satisfying, comes together in just 25 minutes, and uses pantry staples you probably already have, so it works for a busy parent, a hungry student, or anyone who loves good food.

The trick is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, which gives the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything up, and a handful of parmesan brings it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

A wholesome weeknight meal. Serve with extra parmesan on top.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

A new study from researchers at the University of Halden looks at the relationship between napping and memory. The findings, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggest that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The research team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Sleep plays a vital role in healthy aging, and the role of napping in particular is worth further study.

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice was still in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up is only part of it, Cal. She needs to be able to count on you."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for far too long, she thought. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence arising from the combination of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value and the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on a surprisingly elegant principle: destructive interference. They don't just block sound, they fight it with more sound.

Here's how it works. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, dramatically reducing what reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you're a frequent flyer, a remote worker, or just someone who likes peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a better pair.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line. The plan adds 11 new stops and extends service hours to midnight.

"This is about giving people a real alternative to driving," said Supervisor Lena Kowalczyk, who sponsored the measure. "For a lot of families in the east county, the bus is the only way to get to work."

Supervisor Mark Deaver, who cast the lone dissenting vote, argued that the plan relies too heavily on state matching funds. "If Sacramento pulls back, we're left holding the bill," he said.

According to a 2024 county survey, 38% of east county households do not own a car. Ridership on Route 9 has grown 22% since 2022, reaching roughly 6,400 weekday boardings.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

## Getting Started

**lintwise** is a fast, lightweight, configurable linter for YAML files. Whether you're managing Kubernetes manifests or CI pipelines, it catches errors before they reach production.

### Installation

lintwise requires Python 3.10 or later. Install it with pip:

```bash
pip install lintwise
```

### Usage

Point lintwise at a file or directory:

```bash
lintwise check ./config
```

By default, lintwise checks indentation, duplicate keys, and trailing whitespace. To customize the rules, create a `.lintwise.toml` file in your project root. lintwise exits with code 1 if it finds any errors, so it's easy to add to a CI workflow.

Last spring, at thirty-four, I finally decided to learn to swim. For years I had avoided pools, lakes, and beaches, quietly ashamed that I couldn't do something everyone else seemed to have learned as a kid. Signing up for adult lessons at the YMCA felt like a small act of courage.

But week by week I got better. By June I could swim one slow length of freestyle without stopping. It wasn't pretty, but it was mine.

Looking back, learning to swim taught me more than a physical skill. It's never too late to face your fears, and growth begins at the edge of your comfort zone.

Marcus found his brother on the back porch, looking out at the dark orchard. It smelled of rain and overripe apples, and the crickets were going in the tall grass.

"So you're really selling," Marcus said.

Daniel didn't turn around. "The bank isn't giving us a choice. Dad left us more debt than trees."

Marcus had to wait a second before he could answer. "This orchard was his whole life. We grew up here. It isn't just land, Danny. It's us."

"I know." Daniel's voice cracked. "But holding on won't pay the mortgage. Sometimes letting go is the only way to honor what someone built."

Marcus sat down beside him on the worn steps. Neither of them spoke for a long time. Somewhere in the orchard, an apple dropped.

"Okay," Marcus said at last. "But I'm keeping his pruning shears."

Daniel laughed, a small, broken sound, and Marcus knew they would be all right.

Welcome to _The Rust Programming Language_, an introductory book about Rust. The Rust programming language helps you write faster, more reliable software. High-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds in programming language design; Rust challenges that conflict. By balancing powerful technical capacity and a great developer experience, Rust gives you the option to control low-level details (such as memory usage) without all the hassle traditionally associated with such control.

## Who Rust Is For

Rust suits many people, for a variety of reasons. Let’s look at a few of the most important groups.

### Teams of Developers

Rust is proving to be a productive tool for collaborating among large teams of developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge. Low-level code is prone to various subtle bugs, which in most other languages can only be caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced developers. In Rust, the compiler acts as a gatekeeper, refusing to compile code with these elusive bugs, including concurrency bugs. By working alongside the compiler, the team can spend its time on the program’s logic rather than chasing down bugs.

Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:

- Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding, compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust ecosystem.
- The `rustfmt` formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across developers.
- The Rust Language Server powers integrated development environment (IDE) integration for code completion and inline error messages.

By using these and other tools in the Rust ecosystem, developers can be productive while writing systems-level code.

The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is *always* hungry.

He is always poor, out of luck and friendless. The meanest creatures despise him, and even the fleas would desert him for a velocipede. He is so spiritless and cowardly that even while his exposed teeth are pretending a threat, the rest of his face is apologizing for it. And he is so *homely*!—so scrawny, and ribby, and coarse-haired, and pitiful. When he sees you he lifts his lip and lets a flash of his teeth out, and then turns a little out of the course he was pursuing, depresses his head a bit, and strikes a long, soft-footed trot through the sage-brush, glancing over his shoulder at you, from time to time, till he is about out of easy pistol range, and then he stops and takes a deliberate survey of you; he will trot fifty yards and stop again—another fifty and stop again; and finally the gray of his gliding body blends with the gray of the sage-brush, and he disappears. All this is when you make no demonstration against him; but if you do, he develops a livelier interest in his journey, and instantly electrifies his heels and puts such a deal of real estate between himself and your weapon, that by the time you have raised the hammer you see that you need a minie rifle, and by the time you have got him in line you need a rifled cannon, and by the time you have “drawn a bead” on him you see well enough that nothing but an unusually long-winded streak of lightning could reach him where he is now. But if you start a swift-footed dog after him, you will enjoy it ever so much—especially if it is a dog that has a good opinion of himself, and has been brought up to think he knows something about speed.

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Finding time to cook a nourishing meal on a busy night can feel like an uphill battle. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta is bright and satisfying, comes together in 25 minutes, and uses pantry staples you probably already have. If you're a busy parent, a hungry student, or just someone who loves good food, it will likely end up in your regular rotation.

The key is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, which gives the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

Enjoy.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

Researchers at the University of Halden have looked at the relationship between napping and memory. Their findings, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggest that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Longer naps of more than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Sleep plays an important part in healthy aging, and naps are worth a closer look.

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to give.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept going in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up isn't the whole thing, Cal. She needs someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for too long, she thought, and maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Whether or not this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of two things together: how easy it is to change the way a platform allocates value, and the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on a surprisingly elegant principle: destructive interference. They don't just block sound, they fight it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a pair with more confidence.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line. The plan adds 11 new stops and extends service hours to midnight.

"This is about giving people a real alternative to driving," said Supervisor Lena Kowalczyk, who sponsored the measure. "For a lot of families in the east county, the bus is the only way to get to work."

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and are not well suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

## Getting Started

**lintwise** is a fast, lightweight, and configurable linter for YAML files. Whether you're managing Kubernetes manifests or CI pipelines, it helps you catch errors before they reach production.

### Installation

lintwise requires Python 3.10 or later. Install it with pip:

```bash
pip install lintwise
```

### Usage

Point lintwise at a file or directory:

```bash
lintwise check ./config
```

By default, lintwise checks indentation, duplicate keys, and trailing whitespace. To customize the rules, create a `.lintwise.toml` file in your project root. lintwise exits with code 1 if it finds any errors, so it's easy to add to a CI workflow.

Last spring, at thirty-four, I finally decided to learn to swim. For years I had avoided pools, lakes, and beaches, quietly ashamed of a skill that everyone else seemed to have picked up as kids. Signing up for adult lessons at the YMCA felt like a small act of courage.

The first class was humbling. I clung to the wall while an eight-year-old swam laps in the next lane. My instructor, Gloria, a patient retired teacher, told me to put my face in the water and blow bubbles. My heart pounded. It felt impossible.

But week by week, something shifted. By June, I could swim one slow length of freestyle without stopping. It wasn't pretty, but it was mine.

Learning to swim taught me something far more important than a physical skill: it's never too late to face your fears, and growth begins at the edge of your comfort zone.

Daniel didn't turn around. "The bank isn't giving us a choice. Dad left us more debt than trees."

Marcus's throat went thick. "This orchard was his whole life. We grew up here. It's not just land, Danny. It's us."

"Okay," Marcus finally said. "But I'm keeping his pruning shears."

Daniel laughed, a small, broken sound, and Marcus knew they would be all right.

Welcome to _The Rust Programming Language_, an introductory book about Rust. The Rust programming language helps you write faster, more reliable software. High-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds in programming language design; Rust challenges that conflict. By balancing powerful technical capacity with a great developer experience, Rust lets you control low-level details (such as memory usage) without all the hassle traditionally associated with such control.

## Who Rust Is For

Rust is ideal for many people, for a variety of reasons. Let’s look at a few of the most important groups.

### Teams of Developers

Rust is proving to be a productive tool for collaboration among large teams of developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge. Low-level code is prone to various subtle bugs, which in most other languages can only be caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced developers. In Rust, the compiler acts as a gatekeeper, refusing to compile code with these elusive bugs, including concurrency bugs. By working alongside the compiler, the team can focus on the program’s logic rather than chasing down bugs.

Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:

- Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding, compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust ecosystem.
- The `rustfmt` formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across developers.
- The Rust Language Server powers integration with integrated development environments (IDEs) for code completion and inline error messages.

By using these and other tools in the Rust ecosystem, developers can be productive while writing systems-level code.

The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is *always* hungry.

He is always poor, out of luck and friendless. The meanest creatures despise him, and even the fleas would desert him for a velocipede. He is so spiritless and cowardly that even while his exposed teeth are pretending a threat, the rest of his face is apologizing for it. And he is so *homely*!—so scrawny, and ribby, and coarse-haired, and pitiful. When he sees you he lifts his lip and lets a flash of his teeth out, and then turns a little out of the course he was pursuing, depresses his head a bit, and strikes a long, soft-footed trot through the sage-brush, glancing over his shoulder at you, from time to time, till he is about out of easy pistol range, and then he stops and takes a deliberate survey of you; he will trot fifty yards and stop again—another fifty and stop again; and finally the gray of his gliding body blends with the gray of the sage-brush, and he disappears. All this is when you make no demonstration against him; but if you do, he develops a livelier interest in his journey, and instantly electrifies his heels and puts such a deal of real estate between himself and your weapon, that by the time you have raised the hammer you see that you need a minie rifle, and by the time you have got him in line you need a rifled cannon, and by the time you have “drawn a bead” on him you see well enough that nothing but an unusually long-winded streak of lightning could reach him where he is now. But if you start a swift-footed dog after him, you will enjoy it ever so much—especially if it is a dog that has a good opinion of himself, and has been brought up to think he knows something about speed.

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Cooking a nourishing meal on a busy night is hard. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta is ready in 25 minutes and uses pantry staples you probably already have. It suits a busy parent, a hungry student, or anyone who likes good food, and it will likely end up in your regular rotation.

The trick is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, which gives the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

A new study from researchers at the University of Halden looks at the relationship between napping and memory. The findings, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggest that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps of more than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Sleep plays a vital role in healthy aging, and the humble nap deserves a second look.

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept going in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her chest tightened. Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." It came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up isn't enough, Cal. She needs someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for far too long, she realized, and maybe, just maybe, she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."
